title: Drill 4 · Term 3 Fix-Up 🔍
subject: Maths
source_note: Test_Analysis_2026-10-02 (Year 7 Term 3 Test 1, 74/100): every question that lost marks — P1 Q13, Q14, Q27, Q28; P2 Q5, Q9, Q10, Q12a/b, Q17. π = 3.14 as in her tests.

questions.stem: Three boxes have an average mass of 15 kg. Each box has a DIFFERENT whole-number mass, and each is at least 12 kg. What is the greatest possible mass of the heaviest box?
questions.explanation: Total = 3 × 15 = 45 kg. To make the heaviest as big as possible, make the other two as SMALL as possible, but they must be different: 12 kg and 13 kg = 25 kg. Heaviest = 45 − 25 = 20 kg.
questions.technique: Underline every condition word first: 'different', 'at least', 'whole number'. Then make the others as small (or as big) as the conditions allow.

questions.stem: Four children have an average age of 10 years. Their ages are all DIFFERENT whole numbers, and nobody is older than 13. What is the youngest that the youngest child could be?
questions.explanation: Total = 4 × 10 = 40. To make the youngest as small as possible, make the other three as OLD as possible, but all different: 13 + 12 + 11 = 36. Youngest = 40 − 36 = 4 years.
questions.technique: Smallest possible one → make the others as big as the conditions allow (and different!).

questions.stem: Five different positive whole numbers have an average of 8. What is the largest possible value of the biggest number?
questions.explanation: Total = 5 × 8 = 40. Make the other four as small as possible AND different: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. Largest = 40 − 10 = 30.
questions.technique: Average × count = total. Then 'different' means 1, 2, 3, 4 … not 1, 1, 1, 1.

questions.stem: A club has 80 members and 35% of them are girls. Then 20 more girls join the club. What percentage of the club are girls now?
questions.explanation: Girls at first: 35% of 80 = 28. After: 28 + 20 = 48 girls. But the club ALSO grew: 80 + 20 = 100 members. 48 out of 100 = 48%.
questions.technique: When people join or leave, BOTH the part and the total change. Write 'new part ÷ NEW total'.

questions.stem: A class has 30 students and 60% are boys. Some new girls join (no boys join). Now boys make up 45% of the class. How many girls joined?
questions.explanation: Boys = 60% of 30 = 18, and that does not change. Now 18 is 45% of the new total: 18 ÷ 0.45 = 40 students. Girls who joined = 40 − 30 = 10.
questions.technique: Find the thing that stays the SAME (the boys), then use it to find the new total.
questions.trap: Giving the new total (40) instead of how many joined

questions.stem: A bag has 40 marbles and 25% of them are red. Sam takes out 4 red marbles. What percentage of the marbles left in the bag are red?
questions.explanation: Red at first: 25% of 40 = 10. After: 10 − 4 = 6 red. Marbles left: 40 − 4 = 36. 6/36 = 1/6 = 16 2/3 %.
questions.technique: Taking things OUT also changes the total. New part ÷ new total.

questions.stem: Lily spent 1/4 of her money on a book and then 1/2 of the REMAINING money on lunch. What fraction of her money did she have left?
questions.explanation: After the book she has 3/4 left. Lunch = 1/2 of 3/4 = 3/8. Left = 3/4 − 3/8 = 3/8. (Quick way: 3/4 × 1/2 = 3/8.)
questions.technique: 'Of the remaining' → work on what is LEFT, not the whole. Draw a bar model.
questions.source: Test_Analysis_2026-10-02 P2 Q10; Fractions topic (fraction of remainder)

questions.stem: Priya spent 25% of her money on a bag. Then she spent 2/3 of the REMAINING money on shoes. She had $180 left.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: What fraction of her ORIGINAL money did she have left? (e.g. 2/7)

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: How much money did she have at first?

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: How much did the shoes cost?

solution: After the bag: 100% − 25% = 75% = 3/4 of her money is left.
Shoes = 2/3 of that 3/4, so 1/3 of the 3/4 is left: 1/3 × 3/4 = 1/4 of her original money.
(b) 1/4 = $180, so her money at first = 4 × $180 = $720.
questions.technique: Bar model: draw the whole, cut off 25%, then split ONLY the leftover part into thirds.
questions.trap: Treating 2/3 as 2/3 of ALL the money (25% + 66.7% > 90%)
questions.source: Test_Analysis_2026-10-02 P2 Q10 (Robin: 3/5 of the remaining)

asks_for.prompt: Before you start: the 2/3 is a fraction of…
options: The money left after the bag

questions.stem: A farmer sold 3/8 of his eggs on Monday. On Tuesday he sold 40% of the REMAINING eggs. He then had 150 eggs left.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: How many eggs did he have at first?

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: How many eggs did he sell on Tuesday?

solution: After Monday: 1 − 3/8 = 5/8 of the eggs are left.
Tuesday he sells 40% of that 5/8, so 60% of 5/8 is left: 0.6 × 5/8 = 3/8 of all the eggs.
3/8 = 150, so 1/8 = 50 and all the eggs = 400.
questions.technique: Fraction then percentage of the remainder: turn each step into 'what fraction is LEFT', then multiply.

options: All the eggs at the start

questions.stem: Square A and square B overlap. Area of A : area of B = 5 : 3. The overlap is 1/3 of the area of B. What is the ratio of the overlap to the area of the WHOLE figure?
questions.explanation: Let A = 5 units, B = 3 units. Overlap = 1/3 of 3 = 1 unit. The whole figure = 5 + 3 − 1 = 7 units (the overlap is inside BOTH squares, so take it away once). Overlap : figure = 1 : 7.
questions.technique: Whole figure = A + B − overlap. The overlap must only be counted once.
questions.source: Test_Analysis_2026-10-02 P2 Q5; Test_Analysis_2026-07-17 P1 Q14

questions.stem: Rectangles P and Q overlap (see the picture). Area of P : area of Q = 5 : 4. The SHADED part is the part of Q that is NOT inside P, and it is 3/4 of the area of Q.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: What fraction of rectangle P is the overlap? (e.g. 2/7)

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: What is the ratio of the shaded area to the unshaded area of the whole figure? (type like 2:7)

solution: Scale the ratio so the fractions are whole: P = 20 units, Q = 16 units.
Shaded (Q only) = 3/4 × 16 = 12 units. Overlap = 16 − 12 = 4 units.
(a) Overlap ÷ P = 4/20 = 1/5.
(b) Unshaded = all of P = 20 units (P only 16 + overlap 4). Whole figure = 20 + 16 − 4 = 32 = 12 + 20 ✓.
Shaded : unshaded = 12 : 20 = 3 : 5.
questions.technique: Pick a number of units that both fractions divide into. Label the 3 regions: P only, overlap, Q only.
questions.trap: Counting the overlap in both P and Q (12 : 24 = 1 : 2)

asks_for.prompt: The unshaded part of the figure is…
options: All of rectangle P (including the overlap)

questions.stem: A quarter circle has a radius of 20 cm. How long is its CURVED edge? (Use π = 3.14)
questions.explanation: Whole circumference = 2 × π × r = 2 × 3.14 × 20 = 125.6 cm. A quarter of it = 125.6 ÷ 4 = 31.4 cm. (Short cut: quarter arc = π × r ÷ 2.)
questions.technique: Arc = fraction × 2πr. Quarter arc = 2πr ÷ 4 = πr ÷ 2. Don't forget the 2!
questions.trap: π × r ÷ 4 = 15.7 cm (forgot the 2 in 2πr) — exactly the Term 3 slip
questions.source: Test_Analysis_2026-10-02 P2 Q12a (used πr/4; answer came out exactly half)

questions.stem: Find the PERIMETER of this quarter circle. (Use π = 3.14)
questions.explanation: Curved edge = 2 × 3.14 × 14 ÷ 4 = 21.98 cm. Plus the two straight radii: 14 + 14 = 28 cm. Perimeter = 21.98 + 28 = 49.98 cm.
questions.technique: Perimeter of a sector = curved arc + the straight edges. Trace the edge with your pencil.
questions.trap: Giving only the arc (21.98) or using πr/4 (10.99 + 28 = 38.99)

questions.stem: A square has sides of 20 cm. Two quarter circles are drawn inside it, centred at opposite corners, each with radius 20 cm. They make the shaded 'leaf'. (Use π = 3.14)

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: How long is ONE of the curved arcs?

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: What is the perimeter of the shaded leaf?

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: What is the area of the shaded leaf?

solution: (b) The leaf's edge is just the two arcs: 2 × 31.4 = 62.8 cm (no straight sides!).
(c) One quarter circle = 3.14 × 20 × 20 ÷ 4 = 314 cm². Two quarter circles = 628 cm².
Together they cover the whole square (400 cm²) and the leaf is covered TWICE.
questions.technique: Overlap trick: two shapes added together − the whole square = the part counted twice.
questions.trap: (b) adding square sides to the leaf's perimeter; (a) using πr/4
questions.source: Test_Analysis_2026-10-02 P2 Q12a/b (quarter-circle design: arc formula + area left blank)

asks_for.prompt: The perimeter of the leaf is made of…

questions.stem: A circle has a diameter of 40 cm. Two semicircles, each with a diameter of 20 cm, are drawn along its diameter to make the shaded shape. (Use π = 3.14)

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: What is the area of the shaded part?

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: What is the perimeter of the shaded part?

solution: (a) Start with the top half of the big circle: 3.14 × 20 × 20 ÷ 2 = 628 cm².
The small semicircle cut OUT on the left is the same size as the small semicircle ADDED on the right (both 3.14 × 10 × 10 ÷ 2 = 157 cm²).
So the shaded area = 628 − 157 + 157 = 628 cm² — exactly half the big circle.
(b) Trace the edge: big semicircle arc = 3.14 × 20 = 62.8 cm, plus two small semicircle arcs = 3.14 × 10 = 31.4 cm each.
questions.technique: Move pieces: a bit cut out on one side + an equal bit added on the other cancels out. For perimeter, trace the edge with your finger and add every curve.
questions.trap: Using the diameter (40) as the radius; adding the straight diameter to the perimeter
questions.source: Test_Analysis_2026-10-02 P2 Q9 (circle + semicircles, left blank) and P1 Q27 (perimeter of shaded parts)

questions.stem: A square has sides of 40 cm. A semicircle is cut out from the left side and another from the right side (each diameter = 40 cm). What is the perimeter of the shaded part? (Use π = 3.14)
questions.explanation: The shaded edge is: top side 40 + bottom side 40 = 80 cm, plus two semicircle arcs. Each arc = 3.14 × 20 = 62.8 cm, so both = 125.6 cm. Perimeter = 80 + 125.6 = 205.6 cm.
questions.technique: Perimeter of shaded part: only the edges that touch the shading. The left and right sides of the square are no longer on the edge.
questions.trap: Adding all 4 sides (285.6) or only the arcs (125.6)
questions.source: Test_Analysis_2026-10-02 P1 Q27 (perimeter of shaded parts, skipped)

questions.stem: Three identical squares share the corner P, which is on a straight line. Use the angles marked to find x.
questions.explanation: Measure every side from the right-hand line at P. Middle square: 180 − 40 − 90 = 50°, so its lower side is at 50°. The next square sits 20° lower: 50 − 20 = 30°, so its other side is at 30 + 90 = 120°. The first square's side is straight up (90°). x = 120 − 90 = 30°. Short cut: x = 90 − 40 − 20 = 30°.
questions.technique: Squares → every corner is 90°. Write the angle of each side from ONE base line and subtract.
questions.trap: Copying a marked angle (20° or 40°) without the chase
questions.source: Test_Analysis_2026-10-02 P1 Q28 (three squares, abandoned; answer 27°)

questions.stem: Ajay, Blair and Simon each had p cards. Ajay gave 1/4 of his cards to Blair. Then Blair gave 2/5 of ALL his cards to Simon. In the end, Simon had 21 more cards than Blair.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: How many cards did Simon have in the end?

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: How many cards did Blair give to Simon?

solution: Ajay gives p/4: Ajay = 3p/4, Blair = p + p/4 = 5p/4, Simon = p.
Blair gives 2/5 of 5p/4 = p/2: Blair = 5p/4 − p/2 = 3p/4, Simon = p + p/2 = 3p/2.
Simon − Blair = 3p/2 − 3p/4 = 3p/4 = 21, so p = 28.
(b) Simon = 3/2 × 28 = 42. (c) Blair gave p/2 = 14.
Check with numbers: 28,28,28 → Ajay gives 7 → 21,35,28 → Blair gives 14 → 21,21,42. 42 − 21 = 21 ✓
questions.technique: Make a table: one row per step, one column per person. Keep everything in p until the last step.
questions.trap: Taking 2/5 of Blair's ORIGINAL p cards instead of all his cards after the gift
questions.source: Test_Analysis_2026-10-02 P2 Q17 (5-mark card-transfer algebra, not reached)
